title: is meditation Buddhist?
hook: mindfulness before it was a corporate wellness word: the old word underneath the apps

segments.voice: Yesterday: the three jewels, three bows to what wakes you up. Today, the question a lot of people with a meditation app quietly wonder.

Mindfulness is on water bottles, on coloring books, in the employee handbook somewhere between the dental plan and the parking policy. Meditation apps teach it, and some give old Buddhist practices new names along the way: insight meditation, calming meditation. So, is meditation Buddhist? Much of what the apps teach grew out of Buddhist practice. The longer answer starts with the old word underneath, and it turns out to be about remembering.
screen: `MINDFULNESS: ON A WATER BOTTLE.` → `NEW NAMES, OLD PRACTICES.` → `IS IT BUDDHIST?`

segments.voice: The old word is sati, in Pali. A Victorian scholar picked mindfulness to translate it, and the English stuck. Sati is related to a Sanskrit word for memory, so it isn't only paying attention. It's remembering to pay attention, and not letting it slip. The old texts give it a job. A fortress on the frontier has a wise gatekeeper who keeps out strangers and lets in the people he knows. He can only do that if he stays at his post and looks at every face. That gatekeeper, the text says, is sati. Here's what the apps often leave out. In the Buddha's teaching, mindfulness is one part of an eight-part path, sitting beside how you speak, how you act and how you earn a living. It isn't a productivity tool. It's meant to notice everything, even whether what you're doing is kind. So if you already sit with an app, you're practicing something with deep roots. The tradition just sets it in a bigger room.
screen: `SATI — REMEMBERING TO NOTICE` · `THE GATEKEEPER AT THE GATE` · `ONE PART OF AN EIGHT-PART PATH` · `DEEP ROOTS, A BIGGER ROOM` · then, large: `REMEMBER TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest your attention on the breath. When a thought walks up to the gate, and one will, don't chase it and don't slam the gate. Just notice it: thought. Then remember the breath. Each time you remember, that's sati.
Sati. Mindfulness, older and fuller: remembering to notice, the gatekeeper at the gate. Third word on your strand.
Your line: remember to notice. Forgetting isn't failing; remembering again is the practice. Day three.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice sati in sitting meditation, in walking and in daily tasks, often following the four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind and mental patterns; in the tradition it is one part of the eightfold path, alongside ethical speech, action and livelihood.

fork.setup: you're the gatekeeper of a frontier fortress. a stranger walks up. what does the gatekeeper in the old image do?
options: let everyone through. not his business.
know who's who: keep strangers out, let friends in.
fork.reveal: the wise gatekeeper keeps out strangers and admits those he knows. sati is that watchfulness: staying at the gate and seeing who's there.

original.note: Pali: mindfulness, awareness. Related to Sanskrit smṛti, memory.

trapdoor: what you thought: a relaxation technique from an app.
what it means: remembering to notice, one part of a path that also covers speech, action and how you earn a living.
what a scholar hears: sati, cognate with Sanskrit smṛti. T. W. Rhys Davids's 'mindfulness' shaped how English hears it; the gatekeeper is the Anguttara Nikaya's frontier fortress (AN 7.63).

story.title: the bowl of oil
story.text: A man is handed a bowl filled to the brim with oil and told to carry it through a crowd that's cheering for the most famous dancer in the land. Right behind him walks a man with a drawn sword. Spill one drop, he's told, and your head comes off. Would he look at the dancer? The Buddha asks his monks. Not a chance. The bowl of oil, he says, is mindfulness of the body.

wrong.myth: mindfulness was invented for stress relief.
wrong.truth: it's an old translation of sati, remembering to notice; in the Buddha's teaching it sits inside a path that also covers how you speak and act.

think.reveal: deep roots, a bigger room. nobody needs to quit anything to learn where it came from.

notes: Moved from day 9 (sati) to day 3 for the rebuilt week one, where it answers the audience research's 'is meditation Buddhist?' question; tightened to the week-one length and voice. The carry changed from 'notice' to 'remember to notice'.

'Much of what the apps teach grew out of Buddhist practice': hedged, since apps also draw on yoga and clinical programs. Confirm tone is fair to secular and Buddhist practitioners alike.
Rhys Davids and 'mindfulness' for sati: the voice says 'a Victorian scholar'. Confirm.
The gatekeeper simile: AN 7.63. The bowl-of-oil story: SN 47.20 (the man carrying the full bowl between the crowd and the beauty of the land, a swordsman behind him). Confirm both.
